sources.origin: KNX TP1 bus of a single-family house (three floors, annex, garage) recorded without interruption from 2020-03-07 15:26 to 2020-04-13 17:00 UTC by the dataset authors (README 'Collection process'). The README does not name the capture interface or any device model. The line-scan (LS) and device-info (DI) attacks were run on the real installation from IA 1.1.102 and the recorded attack frames and device answers merged into the normal-operation recording with shifted time stamps.

sources.terms: Wireshark test captures, distributed with Wireshark (GPL-2.0-or-later project); no separate licence for the capture files
sources.origin: Wireshark test suite (test/suite_dissection.py, test/suite_decryption.py at the same revision). knxip_coverage, knxip_decrypt_coverage and cemi_coverage are described there as synthetic; knxip_DataSec, knxip_SecureWrapper and knxip_TimerNotify hold single telegrams of unstated origin. The decryption tests use the published test key 00 01 .. 0F (kip.key_1) and the keyring test/keys/knx_keyring.xml.

sources.terms: Attached to a public Wireshark issue (migrated bug 14825, 'Replace KNXIP dissector', 2018) as example captures for the KNXnet/IP dissector; no licence statement
sources.origin: K12 text exports of Ethernet traffic between a test client (192.168.0.100, not identified) and KNXnet/IP devices on 192.168.0.0/24, recorded 2018. Wireshark's test suite (TestDecryptKnxip) points to them as 'realistic (live captured) KNX/IP telegram sequences'. The devices identify themselves in their DEVICE_INFO blocks: ABB IP-Router IPR/S (MAC 00:0c:de:02:80:8e, at 192.168.0.10 and 192.168.0.11) and ABB IPS/S2.1 (MAC 00:0c:de:9e:50:54, at 192.168.0.222); 00:0c:de is ABB's IEEE OUI. No firmware version is in the traffic. The client sends deliberately malformed frames (conformance-style negative cases).
